entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during thunderstorms that lasts a few seconds, then vanishes, sometimes with a bang. It has no accepted explanation.
entries.background: Reports go back centuries, but almost none are backed by photos or instrument readings. Many theories exist and none is generally accepted.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist. His 1837 work on thunder is where the term ball lightning in the scientific literature starts.

entries.name: Stanley Singer
entries.background: Author of the 1971 book The Nature of Ball Lightning, an early major review of the subject.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Physics professor who keeps a Russian database of ball lightning case files, from which six cases here come.

entries.name: Fragmented science
entries.senseHere: Turner's description of ball lightning research: scattered work by individuals collecting reports, theorizing or running lab tests without coordination.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: Austria's network of sensors that locates lightning strokes and records their strength.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: Germany's lightning location service, which detects strokes by their electrical signals.

entries.name: cloud–ground stroke
entries.background: A lightning flash that travels between a cloud and the earth, as opposed to one that stays in the cloud.

entries.name: positive stroke
entries.background: A lightning stroke that carries positive electric charge to the ground. It is much rarer than negative lightning and often much stronger.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist who sat in the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna. He sketched and measured a fireball he saw in 1868.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at Göttingen. As a child in 1951 he saw a ball split into small spheres that left melted patches on asphalt.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: American palaeontologist at Yale, known for dinosaur fossil discoveries. He later led the US National Academy of Sciences.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German experimental physicist. His 1922 experiment with Otto Stern showed that atoms' magnetic orientation comes in discrete steps.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer and later physics professor. He reported to Nature a glowing ball moving down an aircraft aisle in 1963.

entries.name: Pikes Peak
entries.background: A 4302 m mountain in Colorado where Harvard College Observatory ran a weather station from 1874 to 1888.

entries.name: Puy de Dôme
entries.background: An old volcano 1465 m high in central France, with a weather observatory on its summit.

entries.name: Mt Sonnblick
entries.background: A 3106 m Austrian mountain with a weather observatory on its summit, in Salzburg Province.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist in St Petersburg, killed by electricity in 1753 while studying atmospheric electricity. Engravings later showed a lightning ball striking him.

entries.name: Frankenstein
entries.background: Mary Shelley's 1818 novel about a scientist who animates a creature, linked in popular imagination with electricity and dangerous science.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician and founder of modern neurology, working at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris. Sigmund Freud was one of his students.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: Short-lived paralysis and numbness following a lightning strike or ball lightning, as opposed to lasting psychological after-effects.

entries.name: Dorstone tub case
entries.senseHere: A 1936 report from Dorstone, England, of a hot ball falling into a tub of water and boiling it. Researchers used it to estimate a ball's energy.

entries.name: Poughquag glass
entries.senseHere: A 2008 sighting in Poughquag, New York, where measuring how the house's glass glowed under light gave an estimate of the ball's radiation output.

entries.name: Camp Blanding
entries.background: A military base in Florida where a US research group triggers lightning with rockets trailing metal wire.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.senseHere: A 2012 video recording in China of a ball lightning whose light was split into its colour lines. It showed iron, silicon, calcium, nitrogen and oxygen.
